questions.stem: Hitler's foreign policy aims in the 1930s are best summarised as:
options: overturning Versailles, uniting all Germans and winning Lebensraum in the east
regaining Germany's African colonies while avoiding any expansion within Europe
forming a defensive alliance with Britain and France against Soviet communism
restoring the Kaiser's monarchy and the 1914 borders, and then disarming
questions.explanation: Hitler wanted to destroy the Versailles settlement, bring German speakers into one Reich and conquer living space in Eastern Europe at the expense of the Slavs and the USSR. Colonies mattered far less to him than land in the east.

questions.stem: What did the Anschluss of March 1938 achieve for Hitler?
options: the return of the Saar region to Germany after a League-run plebiscite
the transfer of the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia to the German Reich
the return of Memel from Lithuania after a German ultimatum to its government
the union of Austria with Germany, which the Treaty of Versailles had banned
questions.explanation: German troops entered Austria in March 1938 and it was absorbed into the Reich, breaking the Versailles ban on union. The Saar returned in 1935, the Sudetenland in October 1938 and Memel in March 1939.

questions.stem: Why was the German occupation of Prague in March 1939 a turning point in British policy?
options: It had been approved at Munich, so Britain could no longer object to German claims
It brought Italy into the war on Britain's side, making a firm stand possible at last
It showed Hitler's aims went beyond uniting Germans, so Britain guaranteed Poland
It broke the Nazi-Soviet Pact, so Britain could now ally with the USSR against Germany
questions.explanation: Taking the Czech lands, where few Germans lived, showed that Hitler's promises at Munich meant nothing and that his aims were not limited to German speakers. On 31 March 1939 Britain, with France, guaranteed Poland's independence. The Nazi-Soviet Pact came only in August.

questions.stem: The Nazi-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact of 23 August 1939 included a secret protocol that:
options: divided Poland and the Baltic states into German and Soviet spheres
committed the Soviet Union to join Germany in a war against Britain and France
returned all of the former Russian lands in Poland to the Soviet Union at once
pledged German military help to the Soviet Union against Japan in the Far East
questions.explanation: Publicly the two states promised not to attack each other; secretly they agreed spheres of influence that split Poland and placed most of the Baltic states in the Soviet sphere. The pact freed Hitler from the threat of a two-front war when he attacked Poland. It was not a military alliance against the West.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why Stalin signed the pact with Hitler in August 1939?
options: Britain and France had already declared war on Germany, so he needed an ally quickly
He doubted Britain and France would fight, and the pact gave him time and territory
He shared Hitler's aim of destroying Britain's empire and planned a joint invasion
He had been promised Germany's former colonies and wanted ports on the African coast
questions.explanation: Stalin had been left out of the Munich talks, the Anglo-French military mission to Moscow moved slowly, and Poland would not let the Red Army cross its territory. The pact kept the USSR out of war for the moment and gave it eastern Poland and a free hand in the Baltic. Britain and France declared war only after Germany invaded Poland.

questions.stem: Germany withdrew from both the World Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations in:
questions.explanation: In October 1933 Hitler withdrew from the Geneva conference and the League, claiming Germany was denied equal treatment in armaments. Rearmament followed, with conscription announced openly in March 1935.

questions.stem: Why did the Italian invasion of Abyssinia in 1935-1936 badly damage collective security?
options: The League voted to support Italy, so Abyssinia was left without allies of any kind
Britain and France declared war on Italy, which split the League into armed camps
The USA vetoed League sanctions in the Council, so no measures could be taken at all
League sanctions left out oil, and Britain and France sought a deal with Mussolini
questions.explanation: The League imposed limited sanctions but not on oil, and the Hoare-Laval Pact of December 1935 proposed giving Italy much of Abyssinia. Italy completed its conquest in 1936, the League lost credibility and Mussolini moved closer to Hitler. The USA was never a League member.

questions.stem: Which factor helps explain why Chamberlain's government followed a policy of appeasement in 1937-1938?
options: British rearmament was incomplete, and many believed Versailles had been too harsh
Britain had a binding alliance with Germany that was signed after the First World War
The USA had promised to fight Germany if Britain and France stood firm against Hitler
The USSR had refused every offer of talks on collective security in Europe since 1933
questions.explanation: Memories of the First World War, fear of bombing, the cost of rearmament, reluctance in the Dominions and a feeling that some German grievances were fair all pushed Britain towards concessions. The USA was isolationist and made no such promise, and the USSR in fact pressed for collective security in these years.

questions.stem: Revisionist historians defend appeasement mainly by arguing that:
options: it bought time for rearmament, such as radar and modern fighters, before war came
it would have stopped Hitler for good if Churchill had not abandoned it in 1940
Britain and France were already far stronger than Germany, so concessions cost nothing
the League had approved every concession, so appeasement was simply a legal duty
questions.explanation: The orthodox view, set out in the 1940 book Guilty Men, blamed Chamberlain for weakness. Revisionists point to Britain's military and economic limits and argue the time gained helped Fighter Command and radar to be ready by 1940. Few argue that appeasement could have stopped Hitler permanently.

questions.stem: Blitzkrieg is best described as:
options: long sieges of fortified cities, starving the defenders out before any assault
static defence along a fortified line, waiting for the enemy to attack first
a naval blockade to cut an enemy's imports before any fighting on land began
fast attacks massing tanks, motorised infantry and aircraft to break through
questions.explanation: German forces concentrated armour and motorised troops, supported by dive bombers, to break through at a narrow point and drive deep behind enemy lines. Static defence along a fortified line describes the French reliance on the Maginot Line.

questions.stem: Mussolini's main aim in bringing Italy into the war in June 1940 was to:
options: defend Italy from an expected French invasion in the Alps
help the Soviet Union against an expected German attack
deter a British invasion and so keep Italy out of the war
build a Mediterranean empire while France was collapsing
questions.explanation: Italy declared war on Britain and France on 10 June 1940, when France was close to defeat, hoping to gain territory in the Mediterranean and Africa cheaply. Italian offensives in Greece and North Africa soon failed and needed German rescue.

questions.stem: The Atlantic Charter agreed by Churchill and Roosevelt in August 1941 set out:
options: a military alliance under which the USA declared war on Germany straight away
a plan for the Allied invasion of northern France in the summer of the next year
the terms of American Lend-Lease aid to the Soviet Union and the Arctic convoys
shared war aims, such as no territorial gains and self-determination
questions.explanation: The Charter stated principles for the post-war world, including no territorial gains and self-government for peoples. The USA was not yet at war; it entered only after Pearl Harbor and Germany's declaration of war in December 1941.

questions.stem: After Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, the Soviet Union:
options: invaded eastern Poland on 17 September 1939
declared war on Germany two days afterwards
sent military aid to Poland through Romania
stayed neutral and took no Polish territory
questions.explanation: Under the secret protocol of the Nazi-Soviet Pact, the Red Army entered eastern Poland on 17 September. Poland was divided between the two powers. Britain and France, not the USSR, declared war on Germany on 3 September.

questions.stem: Germany's invasion of the Netherlands and Belgium on 10 May 1940 helped its strategy by:
options: drawing the best Allied armies north while the main blow fell in the Ardennes
securing Dutch oil fields that were needed to fuel the Luftwaffe's attack on Britain
opening a sea route to the USSR so that Soviet grain could arrive under the pact
avoiding France entirely, since Hitler planned at that stage to attack only Britain
questions.explanation: British and French forces advanced into Belgium to meet the attack, as Germany expected. The main German armoured thrust came through the Ardennes and cut them off. The Netherlands surrendered on 15 May and Belgium on 28 May.

questions.stem: Which factor best explains the speed of France's defeat in May-June 1940?
options: Britain refused to send any troops at all to France before the German attack began
The Maginot Line was broken by a head-on assault in the first days of the campaign
A thrust through the Ardennes bypassed the Maginot Line and trapped armies in Belgium
France had far fewer tanks than Germany, and none of them could match German designs
questions.explanation: The Allies had comparable numbers of tanks, some of them better than Germany's, but spread them out, while the Germans concentrated theirs and crossed the Meuse at Sedan. The British Expeditionary Force was in France from 1939. France signed an armistice on 22 June 1940.

questions.stem: Operation Dynamo, in late May and early June 1940, was:
options: the British attack on the French fleet at Mers-el-Kebir
the German armoured attack through the Ardennes forest
the evacuation of British and French troops from Dunkirk
the German plan to invade Britain across the Channel
questions.explanation: About 338,000 British and French troops were evacuated from Dunkirk, saving much of Britain's army, though almost all its heavy equipment was lost. The planned German invasion of Britain was Operation Sea Lion.

questions.stem: Operation Barbarossa, launched on 22 June 1941, aimed to:
options: punish the Soviet Union for its declaration of war on Germany in 1940
destroy the Red Army quickly and seize land and resources as Lebensraum
seize Moscow only, then make a peace that left the Soviet Union intact
help Japan by drawing Soviet troops away from Manchuria and from China
questions.explanation: Three army groups attacked towards Leningrad, Moscow and Ukraine, expecting to destroy the Red Army in a few months. The war was ideological and racial, aiming to seize land, grain and oil and to destroy what the Nazis called Judeo-Bolshevism. The USSR had not declared war on Germany.

questions.stem: Why was the RAF's victory in the Battle of Britain in 1940 significant?
options: it persuaded the USA to declare war on Germany by the end of that year
it forced Germany to sign an armistice and give up its gains in France
Hitler postponed Operation Sea Lion, and Britain survived as a base
the Luftwaffe was destroyed and could not fight in any later campaigns
questions.explanation: Without air superiority Germany could not invade, and Sea Lion was postponed in September 1940. Britain survived as a base for later bombing and for the 1944 invasion. The Luftwaffe was weakened but went on fighting, and the USA entered the war only in December 1941.

questions.stem: Which factor contributed most directly to the RAF's success in the Battle of Britain?
options: American heavy bombers attacking Luftwaffe airfields across France
Soviet fighter squadrons based in southern England during the battle
a German decision to send its bombers over without fighter escorts
radar and a control system that directed fighters to incoming raids
questions.explanation: Radar stations and the Dowding system of operations rooms let Fighter Command meet raids without wasting fighters on patrols. Hurricanes and Spitfires fought over home territory, so many shot-down pilots could fly again. German bombers usually had fighter escorts.

questions.stem: On 7 September 1940 the Luftwaffe switched its main attacks from RAF airfields to London. Why do historians often see this as a German mistake?
options: It brought the Soviet Union into the air war over Britain on the British side
London had no anti-aircraft guns, so the raids failed to cause any damage at all
It relieved the pressure on Fighter Command just as its losses were becoming serious
It meant the Luftwaffe stopped bombing other British cities for the rest of the war
questions.explanation: Attacks on airfields and sector stations had been wearing down Fighter Command. The switch to London gave the RAF time to repair bases and recover. The Blitz went on to hit many cities, including Coventry, Liverpool and Glasgow.

questions.stem: The Blitz of September 1940 to May 1941 affected British civilians by:
options: killing tens of thousands, destroying homes and testing morale in many cities
forcing the government to evacuate the whole population of London to Canada
ending rationing, since imported food could no longer reach British ports
persuading most Britons to support a negotiated peace settlement with Germany
questions.explanation: Night raids killed tens of thousands of civilians and left many homeless, and people sheltered in Anderson shelters and Underground stations. Morale bent but did not break, and rationing, introduced in January 1940, continued.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the Allied strategic bombing of Germany?
options: It was carried out only at night by the RAF, so it never struck industrial targets
It did not break morale but tied down fighters and guns and wrecked oil and transport
It broke German civilian morale by 1943, and the regime then asked for peace terms
It had no effect on German industry, since every factory had been moved underground
questions.explanation: RAF area bombing under Arthur Harris and American daylight raids devastated cities such as Hamburg in 1943 and Dresden in 1945, but did not break morale. Bombing forced Germany to keep many fighters and anti-aircraft guns at home, and attacks on oil and transport in 1944-1945 crippled its war economy.

questions.stem: The siege of Tobruk in Libya in 1941 is remembered in Australia because the town was largely defended by:
options: the US 1st Armored Division
the Free French 1st Brigade
the Australian 9th Division
the New Zealand 2nd Division
questions.explanation: The 9th Division held Tobruk against Rommel's forces from April 1941, earning the name 'Rats of Tobruk', before most of it was relieved by sea later that year. Holding the port threatened Rommel's supply lines into Egypt.

questions.stem: Why were the Second Battle of El Alamein (October-November 1942) and Operation Torch together a turning point in North Africa?
options: Italy surrendered at once, which allowed the Allies to land in Italy without opposition
the Soviet Union sent armies into Egypt, opening a third front against the Axis powers
Axis forces were caught between two Allied armies and surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943
Rommel was captured, and German resistance in North Africa ended within a week or so
questions.explanation: Montgomery's Eighth Army defeated Rommel at El Alamein, and on 8 November 1942 Anglo-American forces landed in Morocco and Algeria. Squeezed from both sides, Axis forces surrendered in Tunisia in May 1943, securing the Suez Canal and opening the way to Sicily and Italy.

questions.stem: Why was the Battle of Moscow (October 1941 to January 1942) a turning point?
options: Japan joined the German attack on Moscow and suffered a decisive defeat there
A Soviet counter-offensive in December 1941 ended German hopes of a quick win
The German army captured Moscow, but Stalin moved east and kept the war going
The Red Army drove all German forces out of the Soviet Union by early 1942
questions.explanation: German forces reached the outskirts of Moscow, but on 5 December 1941 Zhukov counter-attacked with fresh troops, including divisions from Siberia. It was the German army's first major defeat on land, and Germany now faced a long war. Stalin stayed in Moscow.

questions.stem: The Soviet counter-offensive at Stalingrad in November 1942, Operation Uranus, led to:
options: the destruction of German Army Group Centre in Belorussia
the German capture of the Caucasus oilfields around Baku
the encirclement and surrender of the German Sixth Army
the capture of Berlin by the Red Army within three months
questions.explanation: Soviet forces broke through the weaker Romanian armies on the flanks and surrounded the Sixth Army under Paulus. The last German troops surrendered on 2 February 1943. The destruction of Army Group Centre came in Operation Bagration in 1944.

questions.stem: Which statement about the outcome of the Battle of Kursk in July 1943 is most accurate?
options: Germany won the battle but lacked the fuel to exploit its victory before winter set in
the Red Army went on to reach the German border before the end of 1943
Hitler ordered a full retreat from all Soviet territory to defend Germany itself
Germany lost the initiative in the east for good, and the Soviets took the offensive
questions.explanation: The Red Army knew of the German plan, Operation Citadel, and built deep defences that wore down the German attack. Hitler called it off within days, partly because the Allies landed in Sicily on 10 July. From then on the Soviets advanced westwards almost continuously, and the Red Army did not reach the German border until 1944.

questions.stem: Which measure best shows the British government mobilising civilians for total war?
options: banning women from factory work so that men could stay in their essential jobs
abolishing food rationing so that workers could buy more and keep up production
closing every school in 1939 and sending all older pupils to work in munitions
conscripting unmarried women aged 20 to 30 for war work or the services from 1941
questions.explanation: Under the National Service Act of December 1941, unmarried women in this age group were called up and could choose the forces, civil defence or industry. Rationing, evacuation of children and the Home Guard were other parts of civilian mobilisation.

questions.stem: Compared with Britain, Germany was slow to mobilise women for war work. Which reason best explains this?
options: German women were all employed in war factories already, long before the war began
a treaty with Britain banned women's war work in both countries until the war ended
German industry had no shortage of labour at all until the final weeks of the war
Nazi ideology stressed women's role in the home, and foreign forced labour filled gaps
questions.explanation: Nazi ideology saw women mainly as wives and mothers, and the regime feared unrest if it forced them into factories. Instead it relied on millions of foreign forced labourers and prisoners. Only after Stalingrad did Goebbels proclaim total war in February 1943.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of the war on Soviet civilians?
options: Civilian deaths were low because the fighting took place far from the cities
Millions died under occupation, in sieges such as Leningrad, and from hunger
Most civilians were evacuated to Siberia before the German invasion began
German occupation forces generally treated Soviet civilians as their allies
questions.explanation: Nazi racial policy treated Slavs as inferior, and occupation brought mass killing, forced labour and deliberate starvation. Leningrad was besieged from September 1941 to January 1944 and huge numbers died of hunger. Whole factories and their workers were moved east of the Urals to keep production going.

questions.stem: Kristallnacht, on 9-10 November 1938, was:
options: the passing of laws that stripped German Jews of their citizenship
the meeting at which Nazi officials coordinated the 'Final Solution'
the first deportation of German Jews to ghettos in occupied Poland
a nationwide attack on Jewish synagogues, homes and businesses
questions.explanation: Nazi-organised violence across Germany and Austria destroyed synagogues and Jewish shops, killed many Jewish people and led to tens of thousands of Jewish men being sent to concentration camps. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 had already removed Jews' citizenship.

questions.stem: How did Nazi policy towards Jewish people change after the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941?
options: persecution was suspended for a time to avoid provoking the United States
mobile killing units, the Einsatzgruppen, began mass shootings of Jewish people
Jewish people were allowed to emigrate freely to Palestine and the United States
the ghettos in occupied Poland were closed and their inhabitants were released
questions.explanation: Following the army, the Einsatzgruppen and other units shot hundreds of thousands of Jewish men, women and children in the occupied east in 1941. Persecution moved from exclusion and ghettoisation to systematic murder.

questions.stem: The Wannsee Conference of 20 January 1942 was significant because senior officials:
options: planned a scheme to resettle Europe's Jews on Madagascar
coordinated the plan to deport and murder the Jews of Europe
decided to begin the invasion of the Soviet Union that summer
agreed the Nuremberg Laws defining who was legally Jewish
questions.explanation: Chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, the meeting organised cooperation between government agencies in the 'Final Solution'. Extermination camps such as Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor and Belzec carried it out, and about six million Jewish people were murdered in the Holocaust. The Madagascar plan of 1940 had already been dropped.

questions.stem: The Allied landings in Normandy, Operation Overlord, began on:
options: 25 August 1944
6 June 1944
6 June 1943
8 November 1942
questions.explanation: On D-Day, 6 June 1944, American, British and Canadian forces landed on five beaches under the overall command of Eisenhower. Torch began on 8 November 1942, and Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944.

questions.stem: Why did Operation Fortitude contribute to the success of D-Day?
options: It persuaded Hitler to move every one of his Panzer divisions to the Eastern Front
It convinced German commanders that the main landing would come at the Pas de Calais
It destroyed the Atlantic Wall defences along the Normandy coast weeks beforehand
It landed Soviet troops in Norway to draw German divisions away from France
questions.explanation: Fake armies, dummy equipment, radio traffic and double agents persuaded the Germans that Normandy was a diversion. Strong German forces were held back near Calais for weeks, which helped the Allies build up their beachhead.

questions.stem: Which developments in August 1944 completed the liberation of much of France?
options: the fall of Rome and the surrender of the Vichy French army in North Africa
the breakout from Normandy, landings in southern France and the freeing of Paris
the German surrender at Reims and the end of fighting in Italy and the Balkans
the Battle of the Bulge and the crossing of the Rhine at the Remagen bridge
questions.explanation: After the breakout and the Falaise pocket, Allied forces landed in southern France on 15 August, and Paris was liberated on 25 August 1944. The Bulge came in December 1944, the Rhine crossings in March 1945 and Germany's surrender in May 1945.

questions.stem: Operation Bagration, launched by the Red Army in June 1944, was significant because it:
options: lifted the siege of Leningrad after nearly three years of German blockade
captured Berlin and forced Germany's unconditional surrender to the Allies
drove German forces out of the Caucasus and back across the Don River
destroyed Germany's Army Group Centre and carried the Red Army into Poland
questions.explanation: Attacking in Belorussia, where the Germans did not expect the main blow, Soviet forces shattered Army Group Centre and advanced to the Vistula by August. Coming just after D-Day, it meant Germany could not send reinforcements to both fronts. Leningrad's siege had ended in January 1944.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains the Allied victory in Europe?
options: an atomic bomb used against Germany, followed by a German revolution in 1944
the Allied capture of Berlin in 1943, and Germany's lack of tanks and aircraft
Allied industrial and manpower superiority, Soviet sacrifice and Hitler's errors
German troop shortages from 1939, and Italy's early surrender to Britain in 1940
questions.explanation: The USA, USSR and British Empire together far out-produced Germany, Lend-Lease supported Britain and the USSR, and the Red Army did most of the fighting against the German army. Hitler's decisions, such as fighting on two fronts and banning retreats, added to Germany's defeat.

questions.stem: Which decision by Hitler is often cited as a strategic error that helped the Allies win?
options: signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact, which kept the Red Army entirely out of Poland
withdrawing all German forces from North Africa in 1941 to defend France
refusing to attack France in 1940 and waiting for a British attack instead
declaring war on the USA in December 1941 while still fighting the USSR
questions.explanation: Germany declared war on the USA on 11 December 1941, bringing the world's greatest industrial power fully into the European war while the German army was stalled before Moscow. The Nazi-Soviet Pact actually brought the Red Army into eastern Poland.

questions.stem: The Lend-Lease Act passed by the US Congress in March 1941 contributed to Allied victory by:
options: lending captured German gold reserves to Britain to pay for its weapons
requiring Britain to hand over its colonies in return for American ships
letting the USA supply war materials to Britain and, later, the USSR
sending American troops to fight in North Africa during the same year
questions.explanation: Lend-Lease let the president lend or lease weapons, food and equipment to countries whose defence mattered to the USA, without cash payment. Aid to the USSR included vast numbers of trucks, helping the Red Army's advances. American troops first fought in North Africa in November 1942.
